And Down Again

Powell loses a second straight, posts his lowest score of the year, and the fix for it has been sitting on his own bench the whole time.

83.2. That is what the defending champion scored on Sunday, and it is the worst number he has put up all season. James Lombardi beat him 97.1 to 83.2 while leaving 77.6 points on his own bench, which should tell Darryl Powell everything about how little was asked of the winner. It is his second defeat in a row, and the two together have turned a one–man race into a four–man one: Powell, Counihan, Flanagan and Haas are all 4–2, with five more teams at 3–3 behind them. He is still the favourite — still first in points for at 700.9, still the strongest roster in the league at 115.1 a week, still 28% to repeat. But Jonathan Taylor’s 20.1 was the best any History Maker managed on Sunday, and behind Taylor the running back room is one injury from nothing — the full analysis is below, and it is not comfortable reading. Elsewhere the week was unrecognisable. Eric Counihan scored 69.4, forty points below anything he had managed all year, and went out of Survivor — six remain. Kevin Flanagan put up 151.2 and joined the group at the top. Patrick Hanna won a third straight and has gone from 0–3 to 3–3 in a month. And Ken Tinkham won a football game, 120.2, his best of the year, in the second straight week he has set a near–perfect lineup. The wire was busy and bought almost nothing: $34 across seven winning claims moved three lineups by a point or less. Week 7 sends Flanagan and his 151.2 to Powell and his 83.2.

The champion’s problem, in four numbers

The model still rates this the best roster in the league. That is exactly why the last two weeks should worry him — he is losing with the best team, and the reasons are specific and fixable.

The numberWhat it is
20.1Jonathan Taylor’s score, and the highest any History Maker posted in Week 6. Nobody else cleared 15.
109.7What this roster is worth the week Taylor misses one — down from 115.1, and from first in the league to third. Behind Taylor: Kyle Monangai (RB28, out), Jadarian Price (RB45, injured reserve) and Dameon Pierce, the 75th–ranked back in football.
241The trade value sitting on his bench in Patrick Mahomes (QB8) and Travis Kelce (TE8) — two positions where he already starts a top–six player in Joe Burrow and Tucker Kraft.
1.3Brian Haas’s quarterback value per week, the worst in the league, with Lamar Jackson on injured reserve. James Lombardi — the man who just beat Powell — is second worst at 3.2 with Jalen Hurts on IR. Both are 4–2. Both have a running back to spare: Tony Pollard (RB26) and Rhamondre Stevenson (RB20).

Put those together and the deal writes itself. Powell is carrying a spare top–eight quarterback that two of the three teams level with him desperately need, and both of them have the running back he is missing. He spent Wednesday instead chasing receivers — bid on Stefon Diggs, bid on Omar Cooper Jr., lost both, and settled for DeMario Douglas, the 60th–ranked receiver in football. He is shopping in the wrong aisle.

The wire

Everything that has moved since the last edition.

Thu 16 – Sun 18 Oct. Powell cut Brian Robinson Jr. for Dameon Pierce. Nairn took Kirk Cousins off free agency, dropping Jacoby Brissett — the quarterback he had paid $15 for two weeks earlier — and then let Stefon Diggs go for nothing. Haas added Harrison Butker. Lombardi dropped Mark Andrews to win Brenton Strange, then dropped Strange three days later for Hunter Henry.

Wed 21 Oct, cleared at 12:04am. Seven winning claims, $34 between them, and five failed ones. Nairn spent $15 on Omar Cooper Jr. and $5 on Chris Boswell — $20, the most anyone has spent in a single run this season. Quincey went $6 on Aaron Rodgers and $4 on Tyler Allgeier, then dropped Allgeier the same night. Flanagan $3 on the Jets defense, cutting the Chiefs defense he had bought for $6 the week before. Walker $1 on Alec Pierce. Powell took DeMario Douglas for nothing after losing on Diggs and Cooper.

And after it cleared. Quincey picked up Stefon Diggs free, four days after Nairn dropped him, and changed defenses again — Colts out, Browns in, his third defense in three weeks. Walker swapped kickers. B. Clemens swapped kickers. Lombardi dropped Jameis Winston.

$34 across seven winning claims, and the needle barely moved. Rebuild every starting lineup before and after and the whole league gains two points a week between twelve teams: Quincey +1.0 and Nairn +1.0 are the only ones worth a sentence, and Nairn paid $20 for his. Flanagan went backwards by half a point buying a defense to replace the defense he bought last week. The one genuinely free win of the fortnight was Quincey taking Stefon Diggs off the wire for nothing four days after Nairn dropped him.

Storylines through six weeks

Darryl Powell has lost two in a row and scored his lowest number of the season doing it, which has turned the title race into a four–way tie. Eric Counihan went from beating Powell to the lowest score in the league in eight days, and out of Survivor with it. Patrick Hanna has won three straight after starting 0–3. And Ken Tinkham finally won a football game, in the second week running he set a near–perfect lineup.

The champion is losing with the best roster, and the answer is on his bench

Powell is 4–2 after 124.5 and 83.2, still first in points for and still the strongest team in the league at 115.1 a week. The problem is not the top of his roster, it is the shape of it: Jonathan Taylor is his only startable back, and behind Taylor sit a man who is out, a man on injured reserve and the 75th–ranked running back in football. The week Taylor misses, this roster is worth 109.7 and it is third in the league, not first. Meanwhile Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce are on his bench behind a top–five quarterback and a top–six tight end, and the two teams level with him at 4–2 have the two worst quarterback rooms in the league.

Tinkham won, and he won the right way

120.2, his best of the season by eighteen points, and 8.4 left on the bench — the second straight week Staff Infection has set close to a perfect lineup, after wasting only 7.0 in Week 5. The decisions have been right for a fortnight; this is the week the roster cooperated. It does not change the arithmetic much — 1% for the playoffs, 71% for the wooden spoon — but the man who picked himself to win it in August is no longer the only owner without a win.

Hanna has moved eight places, and still never won anything

0–3 on 92.1, 87.0 and 85.2. Then 120.9, 119.8 and 114.7, and three straight wins. Same roster, same receivers, the best contract in the league in Ja’Marr Chase at a 4th. ESPN has moved him eight places up its board in a fortnight, further than any owner has moved all season, for doing nothing differently. He is 3–3 and 52% to reach the playoffs. He is also the worst drafter in the history of this league at −2170 and its second–best keeper manager at +972, which is the whole character in two numbers: nobody is better at acquiring value and nobody has converted less of it. Sixteen seasons, one final, no titles.

Two records that do not match their teams

Sean Quincey is 3–3 with the second–best roster in the league at 111.3 a week and a 12% title chance — higher than Flanagan or Haas, who are both 4–2. Brian Clemens is 2–4 with the third at 109.8. Between them they have the clearest schedule–luck gaps on the board. Going the other way, Kevin Clemens has scored 666.7, third–most in the league, on a roster the model rates tenth. 02 / The fiction desk

Things that did not happen

The man who faded in the week he was favourite, and the man who never changed and finally won. Both interviews are invented. Nobody said any of this.

⚠ Everything in this chapter is fiction. The interviews never took place. The quotes were invented. No owner said, thought, or did any of what follows. The only real things here are the scores — and they are quite bad enough on their own.

Invented · Nobody said this · Fiction

“I beat Darryl Powell. Eight days later I scored sixty–nine. You do not get to have both.”

The Faded Power talked this time. That is the first thing worth reporting. Two weeks ago he answered four questions with the word yes and one with the word no; on Sunday he scored 69.4 and went out of Survivor, and now he will not stop.

By our correspondent · A conversation that never occurred · The same very tidy kitchen, less tidy

The list is still on the refrigerator. Something has been crossed out.

Sixty–nine point four.

“Say the rest of it.”

The lowest score in the league this week.

“Say the rest of it.”

Forty points below anything you had scored all season.

“There it is. One hundred and twenty–five, one hundred and nineteen, one hundred and eighteen, one hundred and nine, one hundred and forty–four. And then sixty–nine point four. That is not a bad week. A bad week is ninety. That is a building coming down.”

Eight days earlier you went to Darryl Powell’s place and beat him.

“Fourteen times in seventeen he has beaten me. Fourteen. I have been losing to that man since before some of these owners could drive. And I went there, and I scored a hundred and forty–four, and I took his unbeaten record off him, and for about six days I was the second favourite to win this thing.”

And then.

“And then Tyler Warren scored zero. Not two. Not one. Zero. And Dak Prescott was my leading scorer with fifteen points, which is not a sentence a serious person says out loud.”

You had 5.7 points on your bench.

“That is the part I want written down. I did not leave anything behind. There was nothing behind. I played every man I had and the men I had scored sixty–nine point four. You can forgive a mistake. There was no mistake.”

This guide calls you The Faded Power.

“I know what it calls me. The trophies are real, the recent form is not. Two thousand and ten. Two thousand and thirteen. Thirteen years. And every season somebody says the old man looks lively again, and then one Sunday arrives and reminds everybody why the name is the name.”

You are still 4–2. Second in points for. Eighty–three percent to make the playoffs.

“Sure.”

Sixteen percent to win it. Second best in the league.

“Sure.”

There he is.

“It does not count for anything until December. That is the whole lesson of being me. I have had good Octobers. I have a shelf of good Octobers.”

He looks at the refrigerator.

“And now I am out of Survivor, in the week I was second favourite, with the lowest score in the league. Ken Tinkham won a football game on the same afternoon. Think about the shape of that.”

FICTION. Eric Counihan did not say any of this and no such conversation took place. The real parts: he is The Faded Power in this guide — championships in 2010 and 2013, none since, and Darryl Powell leads their all–time series 14–3. He really did beat Powell 144.7–124.5 in Week 5 to end the last unbeaten record in the league, and really did score 69.4 in Week 6, the lowest score in the league that week and more than forty points below his previous season low, losing 96.0–69.4 to Jon Nairn and going out of Survivor as the sixth man eliminated. Tyler Warren returned 0.0; Dak Prescott’s 15.2 was his top score; 5.7 points sat on his bench. He is 4–2, second in points for, with an 83% chance of the playoffs and 16% at the title. Ken Tinkham really did win his first game the same afternoon. Everything in quotation marks was invented.

Invented · Nobody said this · Fiction

“Sixteen years of putting things in. Nobody has ever got anything out.”

The Vault has won three in a row and climbed eight places, further than anyone has moved this season. He has also never won this league, which is the longer and more interesting fact, and the one he would rather discuss.

By our correspondent · A conversation that never occurred · Across a desk, with a folder on it he does not open

He has brought a folder. He sets it down. He never opens it. We are fairly sure this is deliberate.

Three in a row.

“Ninety–two, eighty–seven, eighty–five. Then a hundred and twenty, a hundred and nineteen, a hundred and fourteen. Same roster. Same men. Nobody arrived.”

You have moved eight places in a fortnight. The largest move anybody has made this season.

“For doing nothing. That is my whole career in one sentence and you have just said it back to me like it is good news.”

Explain the name, then.

“The guide says I am The Vault because nobody has cracked it yet. Everyone reads that as a compliment. Nobody has cracked it. Including me. I am not the man guarding the vault. I am the man outside it.”

Sixteen seasons.

“Sixteen. Every one of the ESPN–era seasons, all of them, never missed. Four playoff trips. One final. Ninety–two wins and a hundred and twenty–five losses. And in that record book of yours there is a line that says longest wait, never won, sixteen seasons, and it has my name on it.”

2023.

“A hundred and seven point three to ninety–four point nine. Sean Quincey. He writes this newsletter, you know. That is the only final I have ever reached and the man who beat me in it does the typing.”

Here is the part I do not understand. You are the second–best keeper manager in the history of this league, plus nine hundred and seventy–two. And the worst drafter in it, minus two thousand one hundred and seventy, nineteenth of nineteen.

He puts one hand flat on the folder.

“Now you have it. I am excellent at acquiring things and historically incapable of turning up in August and choosing correctly. I fill it. I have never once opened it. Ja’Marr Chase at a fourth is the best contract anybody holds and it will still be the best contract anybody holds in January, when I am watching.”

You graded an A this year. Second of twelve.

“The first time. Sixteen attempts and the first time.”

So this might be it.

“I left fifty–two points on my bench on Sunday and won by fifteen. I left thirty–nine the week before and won as well. Ninety–odd points of value sitting there unused across two victories.”

That sounds like a man who can afford it.

“It sounds like a vault. Full, and shut, and sixteen years old.”

He picks up the folder, still closed, and leaves.

FICTION. Patrick Hanna did not say any of this and no such conversation took place. The real parts: he is The Vault in this guide — “because nobody has cracked it yet.” He has played all sixteen ESPN–era seasons, is 92–125 all time for a .424 win rate with four playoff trips, and has never won this league; the record book lists him under longest wait, never won — 16 seasons. His one final was 2023, lost to Sean Quincey 107.3–94.9. He really is the worst drafter in league history at −2170, nineteenth of nineteen, and the second–best keeper manager at +972; his 2026 draft weekend graded A, second of twelve, and he holds Ja’Marr Chase at a 4th–round cost, the best contract in the league. He started 0–3 on 92.1, 87.0 and 85.2, then won three straight on 120.9, 119.8 and 114.7 to reach 3–3, climbing eight places in ESPN’s rankings — the largest move by any owner this season. He left 52.4 points on his bench in Week 6 and 39.6 in Week 5, winning both. Everything in quotation marks was invented, including the folder.

Want the desk to come for you next? Win something, or lose something dramatically. Both work.

03 / The rest of the season

Where this is all heading

Six weeks in: every roster repriced, the playoff race as it actually stands, and the two markets still open to you.

Every roster repriced on this week’s rest–of–season rankings, dropped into its owner’s best lineup — one quarterback, one back, two receivers, a tight end, a back–or–receiver flex, a kicker and a defense — with six weeks of results carried in and the remaining eight weeks run forward twenty thousand times.

Two defeats have not cost Darryl Powell the top line. He is still the strongest roster at 115.1 a week, still 93% to reach the playoffs and 28% to win it, and still first in points for. What the defeats have cost him is the gap: four teams are level at 4–2 and the title is no longer a one–man conversation. The two records that do not match their teams are both worth watching. Sean Quincey is 3–3 with the second–strongest roster in the league at 111.3 a week and 12% at the title — better than the two 4–2 teams below Powell. Brian Clemens is 2–4 with the third at 109.8 and still 36% to make the playoffs. Meanwhile Kevin Clemens is 3–3 having scored 666.7, third–most in the league, and the model rates his roster tenth — the exact opposite problem. At the bottom, Ken Tinkham won and it changed almost nothing: 1% for the playoffs, 71% for the wooden spoon. Jon Nairn is 2–4 and now second favourite for last at 15%.

04 / The twelve owners

The book on everybody

Twelve characters, one card each: the story, the pair he locked, the grudge he cannot escape.

Sixteen years, 1,260 games, 2,776 draft picks, 143 trades and 895 waiver claims on record — run back through twelve men and what they did with them. Who each of you actually is when the record is laid out end to end — and, now that the rosters are real, what this week and this season look like from your chair. That is the cast. The rest of this book is what they do about it.

Nobody gets the benefit of the doubt here and nobody gets buried. The archetype, the projection and every number underneath them come out of the same place: what you have actually done, every September since 2010. A man who says he drafts for value and then spends fourteen straight first rounds on running backs is a man who drafts running backs.

The player cards below introduce the characters in this epic, and chronicle sixteen years of feuds. Darryl Powell is The Champion — defending champion at 12–2, holding Jonathan Taylor and CeeDee Lamb, the best keeper pair ever declared here. Sean Quincey is The Five Timers Club — five rings, and 48 trades, more than anyone; when the phone rings, it is him. Kevin Flanagan is The Dynasty — three titles, a 16–15 blood feud with Brian Haas across 31 meetings, and the 1,777.8–point season that somehow won him nothing. Brian Haas is The Gambler — the worst draft record in the league and the second–biggest keeper haul in it, which tells you exactly how he plays. Dannie Walker is The Broker — two titles, four more finals lost, one of them to Sean Quincey by nine–tenths of a point.

Patrick Hanna is The Vault, because nobody has cracked it yet — sixteen seasons, zero titles, and Ja'Marr Chase at a 4th, the single best contract in the league. Kevin Clemens is The Metronome — the only owner whose keeper record is essentially flat; he wins it at the draft table or not at all. Brian Clemens is The Bridesmaid — a title so old it predates the ESPN records, and George Pickens at a 5th as his way back. Eric Counihan is The Faded Power — two early titles, none since 2013, and Darryl Powell has beaten him fourteen times in seventeen tries. Ken Tinkham is The Draft Savant — the best open–draft owner in league history, six trades in seven years, and not one final to show for any of it. James Lombardi is The Assassin — the 2024 title from ninth on the board that nobody saw coming, and this year the smallest keeper haul in the league, bought in the last 72 hours; he lives on the draft board. And Jon Nairn is The Understudy — 2–12 last year, years in the wings, then the August trade with Beans that took his keepers from dead last to seventh overnight. Every card below ends with the opponent its owner cannot afford to lose to — in this league you never play a stranger.

Pick a name below to read one at a time, or show all twelve. Cards are ordered by 2026 keeper haul, which is as close to a preseason power ranking as this league has. Each one carries an archetype, a projected finish with the reasoning attached, a scouting report on how he drafts, trades and bids, and the rivalries he cannot escape. Argue with any of it — but argue with the numbers, because that is all this is.

Runner–up in 2025, and nobody worked the deadline like him. The Bowers heist was already done — a dead Drake London contract flipped to Beans in mid–August — and then at 9:41 on deadline night, with the league manager holding the door open, he sold Zay Flowers to Stu for an 8th–round pick. He sold a contract he could not keep to pay for one he could. Bowers (+306) and Collins (+253) is the fourth–best haul in the league, and the four Rd–1–2 stars go back in the pool.

Last place in 2025 at 4–10, and nobody traded like him since — deal after deal from May through the final hours of deadline day. The last one was the strangest and the smartest — he sold Quinshon Judkins, his best contract, to Patrick Hanna for the 27th pick, then burned that same pick declaring Drake London. Kenneth Walker III burned the 3rd he bought from Jon Nairn on 20 August. Two keepers, both at 3rds, both slots bought with trades, and a haul of 296 — ninth of twelve, a single point behind Counihan. What he kept instead is the draft: three second–round picks and more capital than anyone on the board. The assets were there in 2021 too, when he scored 1,777.8 in the regular season, the most this league has ever recorded, and still went home without the trophy. This time the whole plan is one sharp Sunday.

Nine seasons, six playoff berths, no title and no final — the best resume in the league without a trophy game. And then, for once, the quietest man at the table picked up the phone: on deadline day he bought Travis Etienne from the Guardians for his 6th–round pick and declared him within the hour at an 11th, next to Matthew Stafford at a 13th. Etienne at +181 is now the best contract on the roster, and the pair banks 288 — more than double what Stafford and Rachaad White would have returned. It is only his seventh trade in seven years, and it might be his best. Then, with the roster finally sorted, he renamed the franchise Staff Infection — nine years of patient board–craft, rebranded overnight as a medical event. The draft record says the rest takes care of itself.

The best drafter in the league by the numbers, and the owner of one third–place finish in nine years. Ken wins August by more than anyone and has never once been playing on the last Sunday. Nine seasons, one trade, fifteen FAAB dollars spent across two seasons while everyone else emptied the account: he has decided the draft is the whole game, and the standings have been disagreeing with him politely since 2017.

05 / Trade evaluator

Price it before you send it

Build a trade out of real picks and real players and see what the board says before you send it.

Pick the two owners, build both sides, and see what the board says. Players are now priced on rest–of–season value — what each man is worth per week from here, over the player you would otherwise have to start — because that is what actually changes hands in September. Picks are the 2027 picks, priced by round — the order isn’t set, so every pick in a round is worth the same, on the same scale as the players (see the box below). Numbers first, then history — because the market here has a long memory.

How 2027 picks are pricedOne value per round, on the player scale — my estimate, not a measurement

The 2027 draft order doesn’t exist yet, so nobody knows whether a first-rounder is the 1.01 or the 1.12. Every pick in a round is therefore priced the same: the average of all twelve slots. The values sit on the same scale as the players above (rest–of–season points a week over a replacement starter, times 26), so a pick and a player can be traded against each other directly.

RoundValueRoughly the price of

How I got there. Two views, averaged, then smoothed so each round is worth less than the one before. View one: this year’s 180–pick value chart, averaged across the twelve slots of each round and converted to the player scale using the 132 players who appear in both (a first–rounder is ~645 on the chart and ~210 here). View two: what each round of this year’s draft has actually delivered since: the average rest–of–season value of the twelve players taken in it, counting anyone no longer rostered as zero. Round 1 and Round 2 players can’t be kept next year, so the first two rounds are pure one–year value; rounds 3–9 carry a small keeper premium that is already inside the chart.

What I’m not sure of. These are judgment estimates, good to roughly ±20%. The fit between the old chart and the player scale is loose (it explains about half the variation), and one season of draft results is a small sample. A pick pays off in a different year than a rest–of–season player does; I treated the longer 2027 season and the discount for waiting ten months as a wash. Contenders should pay a little less than the number for picks, sellers a little more. The guide does not track who owns which 2027 pick — it lists every round for every owner, so check ESPN before building a deal around a pick someone may already have moved.

Gives up: 0
Gives up: 0
—
Pick two owners and add something to both sides.

Reading the verdict

The grade is the gap between the two sides as a share of the bigger one. Inside 10% is even — that is noise, and the deal comes down to whether you like the players. Past 25% somebody is paying a premium and should have a reason for it: a contending roster, a hole at a position, a player he rates well above his slot.

Any single number here is good to about ±15%. A gap of thirty points is zero.

What it cannot see

It does not know your bye weeks, your injuries, or that you already have four quarterbacks. It does not know that the man you are trading with needs a tight end badly enough to overpay.

Trading a keeper? He is worth his market value to the other owner, but he is worth surplus to you — and the pick you burn keeping him is a real cost. Check 09 / The keeper grades before you talk yourself into anything.

06 / The rulebook

The rules that decide your season

The three rules that decide seasons here, the dates, and the scoring that is not ESPN’s.

Most of these you know. Three of them are worth more than any waiver claim you will make all year. The scoring is the fourth, and it is worth the most.

2026 calendar

Draft order revealNFL draft weekend (April)
ADP finalization31 July
Keeper deadlineSat 29 Aug, 9:00 pm
Pre–draft trade deadlineSun 30 Aug, 9 pm
DraftSun 6 Sep, 2pm — on Zoom
In–season trade deadlineWed 25 Nov, noon
Last roster movesChampionship game day

Keepers are due the Saturday, trades close the Sunday after, and the draft is the Sunday after that. If you are planning a deal, the date that binds you is 29 August, not draft day.

The lineup you are filling

Eight starters out of a fifteen–man roster: one quarterback, one back, two receivers, one tight end, one flex that takes a back or a receiver, a defence and a kicker, with seven on the bench and one injured–reserve slot on top. Twelve teams start twelve backs, twenty–four receivers and twelve flex spots between them.

That shape is why the pick chart looks the way it does. A league that starts only one back at a fixed slot makes the twentieth–best back roughly as valuable as the thirtieth–best receiver, and it makes a tight end who scores like a receiver genuinely scarce, because there are only twelve of those jobs and no flex to absorb the twelfth.

Money

$100 in. $600 champion, $250 runner–up, $100 third, $100 season high points, $100 Survivor, $50 playoff high points. Pay before the end of week one and you get 50 bonus points.

Keepers, in plain terms

  • Two per team, from last year's final roster, declared at the deadline.
  • Cost is the round he was drafted in. Keeping is free of penalty — you just burn that pick.
  • Round 1 and 2 picks can never be kept. Not by you, not by anyone you trade them to. They are worth nothing before the draft.
  • You can only keep a man once. After his keeper year he must be traded or returned to the pool.
  • Keepability travels. Trade a used–up keeper and his new owner may keep him at his locked cost. This is the engine of the whole market.
  • A player acquired before the keeper deadline burns a keeper year on his new team. Acquired after, he travels with the pick itself.
  • Draft picks are tradeable, current season only.

Waiver adds: the price lock

A waiver pickup costs whatever their average draft position is on the ESPN platform as of 31 July before the draft. That price then locks permanently — it does not reprice each year, and it follows him to new owners. It only resets if he hits the wire again.

That lock is the most under–used thing in this rulebook. A late–summer add who breaks out becomes a cheap contract you can hold, trade, and re–trade for years.

Two rulings worth knowing before you trade

A waiver add priced into Rounds 1 or 2 is keepable — once

If a player you picked up off waivers carried a first– or second–round ADP the next summer, you can still keep him. What happens next is the part that catches people: where a keeper is kept becomes his draft slot for the following year. Keep him at a 1st or 2nd and he is a first– or second–round pick from that moment on, and first and second–round picks can never be kept. So a waiver add who prices into round 1 or 2 buys you exactly one season, and then he is back in the pool.

It has happened ten times since the keeper era began. Only two players have ever been kept at a 1st: Aaron Rodgers (Jon Nairn, 2017) and Alvin Kamara (Joe Nairn, 2018). A 2nd is more common — Doug Baldwin (Eric Counihan, 2017), Dalvin Cook (Brian Haas, 2018), Davante Adams (Brian Clemens, 2018), Jarvis Landry (Ken Tinkham, 2018), Melvin Gordon (Kevin Flanagan, 2018), Justin Jefferson (Ken Tinkham, 2021), Kyren Williams (Kevin Flanagan, 2024), and Bucky Irving (Kevin Flanagan, 2025).

Two keepers at the same cost need two picks at that cost

Keeping is paid for with actual picks. If both of your keepers price out at a 6th, you need two sixth–round picks to declare them both. If you only have one, the second man comes out of your next–highest pick — a 5th — and you choose which of the two is the 5th and which is the 6th.

That choice matters more than it looks, because the round you pay becomes that player's draft slot for next year. Pay the 5th on the man you intend to move on from, and pay the 6th on the one you want to keep cheap in the future. It is also a reason to think twice before trading away a middle–round pick you might need to pay a keeper with.

Our scoring is not ESPN's scoringShow the scoring table and what it changes

And that gap is free money, because ESPN's ADP — the thing our keeper prices are built on — assumes default scoring we do not use. Under our rules, every roster in this league is mispriced somewhere. The ledger finds it.

6Points per passing TD (ESPN default: 4)
0.5Per 10 passing yards — 1 pt per 20, not per 25
0.5Per reception. Half PPR, no TE premium
+3/+5Yardage game bonuses at 100 and 200

Offense

  • Passing: 0.5 per 10 yds · 6 per TD · −2 per INT · +3 for a 300–yard game, +2 more at 400
  • Rushing: 0.1 per yd · 6 per TD · +2 for a 40+ yd TD · +3 at 100 yds, +5 at 200
  • Receiving: 0.1 per yd · 0.5 per catch · 6 per TD · +2 for a 40+ yd TD · +3 at 100, +5 at 200
  • Fumbles lost: −2

Kicking and defense

  • FG: 3 under 50, 5 from 50+, 5 from 60+ · −1 on a miss inside 40 · PAT 1
  • D/ST: 1 per sack, 2 per takeaway, 6 per defensive TD
  • Points allowed: 10 for a shutout, 7 at 1–6, 4 at 7–13, down to −7 at 46+
  • Yards allowed: +5 under 100, +3 at 100–199, +1 at 200–299

What to do with that

Quarterbacks are underpriced by our own keeper system. Six–point passing touchdowns plus a yardage rate 25% above ESPN default means a 30–TD, 4,200–yard passer scores roughly 70–80 more points here than in the format ESPN's ADP is built on — four to five points a week. ADP does not know that. Our keeper costs are derived from ADP. So every QB contract in this league is priced by a market that undervalues the position.

The league has half–figured this out already without saying it out loud. Look at who gets kept over and over: Mahomes six times, Josh Allen five, Kyler Murray three, Lamar Jackson three, Joe Burrow three. Owners here keep quarterbacks at a rate that would look insane in a 4–point league, and they have been right to.

Three edges hiding in the scoring table

1. Buy the QB contract. Josh Allen at a 7th and Jayden Daniels at an 8th are cheaper than they look. Late–round QBs with rushing equity are cheaper still — C.J. Stroud costs a 14th, Jordan Love an 11th.

2. Ceiling beats floor. Yardage bonuses at 100 and 200 pay boom players twice. In a half–PPR format with bonuses, the volatile receiver is worth more than his average suggests.

3. Defenses actually matter. A shutout is worth 10 plus 5 more for yardage suppression. That is a startable–RB week from a slot most of you fill in the last round. Aura Farmers keeping Seattle at a 14th (+59) is not a joke pick.

Scoring taken from the current league settings pages. The point–gap figure above is an estimate on a representative quarterback season rather than a measured league result, so treat it as directional. The valuations elsewhere in this guide are not adjusted for it.

07 / The 2026 draft

The board, as it happened

175 picks on a Sunday afternoon, every one priced against the chart it was spent on — and every one now carrying a 2027 keeper cost.

Season twenty–three’s draft is in the books. Each pick below is priced: the player’s value at his ten–site consensus ADP against the chart value of the slot spent on him. December re–grades every one of them on what the man actually produced, as it has for sixteen years. The last column is tomorrow’s argument: the round each player was taken is now his 2027 keeper cost.

The room’s verdict on the tight end run: Sean Quincey took his own Trey McBride back at #13, a second–round price for a player he could not bear to see cross the room; Eric Counihan sniped Tyler Warren at #25; Ken Tinkham took Pitts at 39, and Brian Clemens — who let Warren go back to the pool rather than keep him — drafted Kittle and Fannin back to back at 67 and 71. Darryl Powell left with Kraft and Kelce. Five owners, five different answers to one question.

The report card, keepers included

A draft weekend is two things: what you paid, and what you own. Value is what you paid against the chart — the keeper haul locked in August plus what Sunday’s board gave or charged, every pick priced at its ten–site consensus ADP. Lineup is what you actually walked out with: your best seven starters, priced the same way. The two are standardized and weighted equally, then the twelve of you are ranked — twelve owners, twelve rungs from A+ down, only last place fails. Darryl Powell tops both columns that matter: the biggest haul, the best lineup, an A+. Patrick Hanna ran the only Sunday within 135 of the chart and is second. Brian Clemens paid full freight on the day and still built the second–strongest lineup in the room — the roster is the point. The room collectively paid the chart 4,583 points on Sunday, because the twenty–four best contracts never touched the board. December re–grades everything on what actually happens.

08 / The record book

The record book — 2004 to 2025

Twenty–two seasons, twelve champions, zero repeats — the wall and everything on it.

Twenty–two seasons. Champions back to 2004; full standings, brackets and scores from 2010, which is where the ESPN league history begins. This is the wall every season since has been trying to put a name on — and the reason a ring here is worth arguing about for the next twenty years.

What the wall says this year

Twenty–two seasons, twelve different champions, and not one back–to–back title — the streak Darryl Powell is carrying into this season. Six owners have won it more than once; the closest final in history was decided by 0.9 in 2019, and the number–one seed has taken just over a third of the titles since 2010. Everything anyone has ever argued about at this table is below.

Going back to the beginning

The first six years (2004–2009) are incomplete. We have the champions, and runners–up for some of them, but not the full standings or playoff brackets. Starting in 2010 the ESPN league page has everything. The all–time table carries titles from 2004 forward and win–loss records from 2010 forward.

The stories the numbers tell

Brian Clemens has lost six championship games. Five of them since 2010 — 2011, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2022, three in a row — and one more in the early years. Nine playoff berths, a .548 win rate, more finals than anyone in league history, and one title, in 2006. Nineteen seasons have gone by since. There is no comparable record here.

Dannie Walker owns the regular season and not much else. Most wins (131), best win percentage (.604), most playoff appearances (12 of the 16 seasons since 2010), most points per game. Two titles. He has been the #1 seed three times and been knocked out three times, including a 12–1 year in 2020 and a 12–2 in 2012.

Sean Quincey converts. Five titles — 2007, 2015, 2017, 2019, 2023 — more than anyone, and the only man in the league eligible for the Five Timers Club. Somebody owes him a smoking jacket. In the ESPN era, where the records are complete, that is four titles from seven playoff berths, the best conversion rate in the league by a distance, plus two more finals. He misses the playoffs more than half the time and wins it a quarter of the time.

 

The 2024 Stu The Assassin run is the outlier of outliers. James Lombardi went 2–11, then 3–11, then 5–9, then 3–11 — and then won the whole thing as a #3 seed. If you are sitting on a bad roster reading this, that is your precedent.

Patrick Hanna has been here for every one of the sixteen ESPN–era seasons for a .424 win rate, four playoff trips and one final (2023). He has also been the third–most–improved team of the last three seasons, finishing 2nd, 5th and 4th.

The best team almost never wins. In the sixteen seasons since 2010 the regular season points leader has taken the title six times, and the #1 seed six times. In 2021 Kevin Flanagan scored 1,777.8 points — the highest regular season ever recorded here — went 12–2, and was beaten by 66 in the semifinal.

Survivor

The side game, and the cruellest hundred dollars in the league. Everybody is in from Week 1. Every week the lowest score goes out, for good, and it does not matter who you were playing or whether you won your actual matchup. Twelve teams, eleven weeks, one man left holding the money.

There is no strategy to it. There is no waiver claim that saves you. You simply have to not be the worst team in the league on any given Sunday for eleven straight Sundays, which sounds easy right up until the week your quarterback goes out in the first quarter.

Dannie Walker owned this thing

Five titles — 2017, then four in a row from 2020 through 2023. Nobody else has more than one. For four consecutive seasons, eleven other owners spent three months trying to not be last and Dannie simply never was.

And then there is Kevin Flanagan, who has finished second twice, in 2023 and 2024, and won it zero times. Twice he has been the last man eliminated. Twice he has watched somebody else take the envelope.

The 2019 mystery, solved

The payout sheet had a hole in it: 2019 blank, and 2018 credited to Sean Quincey. Replaying every week of both seasons under the rules produced a cleaner answer — 2018 belonged to Darryl Powell, and Sean's win was 2019, one year later than the sheet said. The table above uses those years.

It was worth the wait. Sean and Brian Haas were the last two standing in 2019, and Haas went out in Week 11 with 126.1 points — a number that would have won him the week outright in three of the previous ten. He just happened to score it against the one team left that scored more.

Playoff high points

Sean Quincey (2017, 2023), Dannie Walker (2018, 2022, 2025), Darryl Powell (2020, 2021) and Kevin Flanagan (2024).

09 / The vault

Everything that got us here

The offseason, the keeper grades, the draft plans, the price charts and sixteen years of history — folded away, open when you want them.

The season is above. This is the record underneath it: how August was won and lost, what every contract cost, and the history that every argument in this league eventually reaches for.

How August set the tableThe deals, the declarations, and the haul table as it stood on draft morning

The strangest offseason this league has ever had is over. Twenty–four keepers locked at the deadline, five trades landed in the final 72 hours, and one deal slid in at 9:41 pm with the league manager holding the door. Here is where it all landed, as it stood on draft morning.

Three dates you need

Keeper deadline: Saturday 29 August at 9:00 pm
Draft day: Sunday 6 September, 2pm — live on Zoom
In-season trade deadline: Wednesday 25 November, noon

The draft is settled: Sunday 6 September at 2pm, Labor Day weekend, with a Zoom running the whole way through. Camera on, sound on, and bring something to say — half the value of this league is the four hours you spend explaining your picks to eleven people who disagree.

Keepers locked at the deadline on the 29th — extended to 11 pm by the league manager so one last deal could clear. Pre–draft trading closes Sunday 30 August at 9 pm, and then the board is what it is: every keeper now travels with the pick he burned, per the rules below.

This was always going to be a strange year. The keeper rule that makes this league interesting — you can keep a man once, then he has to move or go back in the pool — meant that going into this offseason, ten of the twelve most valuable contracts in the league were held by owners who could not use them. Jaxon Smith–Njigba at an 8th. Ja'Marr Chase at a 5th. Jonathan Taylor at a 6th. CeeDee Lamb at a 6th. All of it dead in the hands of the men holding it — in May.

Then, over four days in late May, four owners figured out the answer at the same time: if my dead asset is your live one and yours is mine, we just swap. Nobody pays anybody. Both sides go from zero to a franchise keeper. It happened three times in seventy–two hours:

Three trades, 72 hoursShow the three swaps in full
DateTradeWhat each side gained, at the pick each keeper finally burned
May 23Josh Allen (Haas) ↔ Patrick Mahomes (Guardians) Guardians +283 / Haas turned a dead 7th into a live 8th
May 25Jaxon Smith–Njigba (Powell) ↔ Jonathan Taylor (Haas) Haas +579 / Powell +469
May 25CeeDee Lamb (Beer) ↔ Ja'Marr Chase (Powell) Powell +420 / Beer +535

Three trades. Roughly 2,000 points of surplus conjured out of nothing, because the alternative for all six players was the draft pool. And May was only the opening act: by the time the deadline extension expired, seventeen players had changed hands since 22 May, five of them in the final 72 hours — DeVonta Smith to Stu on the 27th, then Judkins, Etienne and Flowers all sold on deadline day itself, sellers converting contracts they could not keep into picks they could use. Every table below reflects all of it.

"Keeper haul" is the combined surplus of the two players declared — surplus meaning what the man is worth at his 2026 draft slot, minus the value of the exact pick he burned. "Left unkept" is the best eligible surplus each owner chose not to declare and did not sell.

The first beat of the season

The schedule is out, and it opens with a knife. Week 1 sends the Guardians to Aura Farmers — a rematch of the 0.9–point final of 2019, the closest championship this league has ever played, and the two of them meet again in Week 12. The other openers: Haas at Respect My Conglomerate, Racounihans at Beer is My H2O, Folsom at Love thy Nabers Waddle — Kevin against Kevin, their grudge fixture, straight away — 🏆 The History Makers !!!! at Staff Infection, champion against the best drafter alive, and WHO’S NEXT? at Stu The Assassin. And save the last page for the end: Week 14, the final week of the regular season, is Powell at Hanna — the champion against the man with the best contract in football, with playoff seeds on the table. The plans, as writtenThe pre–draft playbooks — measure every owner against what the board told him to do

Twelve plans, one per owner, built from what you kept, the picks you actually hold after the trades and the keeper burns, how you have drafted for the last sixteen years, and who the board says survives to your turn. Pick a name. Then get to work.

Eric Counihan slot 1 · projected #11 · haul 297

You hold 1.01 and then the turn at 24 and 25 — three of the first twenty–five picks, the best front–loaded position in the league, and all three survived the deadline. That suits you: you are +803 in rounds 1–3 and +758 in 4–7, then you fall off a cliff, −462 and −713 in the back half. Your season is won before round eight. So take the best player on the board at 1.01 and do not overthink it, then use 24 and 25 back–to–back to take two starters rather than one starter and one dart. Breece Hall and Chris Olave are locked in and cost you the 49th and 73rd, which is why your next pick after 48 is 72 — the gap in your middle rounds is the price of the spine. Four straight years out of the playoffs is not a talent problem, it is a back–half problem.

Three things that apply to everybody

Running backs lose money here. Every owner is negative on them, at −27.9 a pick across 751 open selections. That does not mean avoid them. It means stop taking one at your first pick out of habit.

Quarterbacks are underpriced. ADP assumes 4–point passing touchdowns; this league pays 6. Anyone reading the national board is undervaluing the position by roughly a round.

Round one is nearly full value, the middle is not. Only six of the twenty–four keepers are top–24 ADP players, so the board barely moves at the top and then falls off. The keeper tax gets paid in rounds three through eight.

What things are worthThe offseason market and the pick value chart every price comes from

Two halves of one idea: what this league actually paid for keepers and picks in the offseason just finished, and the chart every price in this guide comes from. Read the first before you make an offer; keep the second open on draft day.

What the offseason charged

Nine sales across the 2026 offseason, four of them in the last three days before the deadline, and together they are the best price data this league has ever produced. Read it before you make an offer next August — and before you accept one.

Conventional wisdom says a man who has to sell gets fleeced. The opposite happened, and the closer to the deadline the more true it got. Sellers cleared roughly half to two–thirds of an asset's surplus in the summer trades, kept all of it in the star–for–star swaps, and in the final three days got back 85% to 167% — two of the four late sales returned more pick value than the player’s surplus, because by then the buyers were not paying for surplus, they were paying to avoid declaring the wrong pair. When ten other teams know a good player has to move, the bidding does the seller's work for him.

The rule this implies

Look for the swap first, every time. A trade between two owners who both hold dead assets is the only trade in this format where both sides genuinely win, and it costs neither of them a pick. Only when no swap exists should picks change hands — and then the going rate is high, because the buyer is bidding against ten other teams for a shrinking pool.

Marginal value: the number almost everyone gets wrong

You can only keep two players. So an incoming keeper is not worth his surplus — he is worth his surplus minus the man he pushes out of your top two. That is the whole explanation for deadline week. Zay Flowers at +142 was worth nearly all of it to James Lombardi, whose second–best declaration would otherwise have been a kicker at +47, and worth nothing at all to the teams above him. Rashee Rice at +215 was the best asset on the board and drew no buyer, because the four owners who could have used him were the four least willing to spend a pick.

This is why the same asset drew wildly different offers, and why the bottom of the keeper table did the buying while the top of it sat still. Remember it next August: your surplus is not the price, the gap is.

What the deadline actually cost

Three contracts died where they stood. Rashee Rice at +215, Jayden Daniels at +88 and Courtland Sutton at +30 were all keepable by somebody and kept by nobody. Rice is the largest surplus this league has ever let expire. Every one of them had a buyer with room — Stu bought twice in 72 hours and still did not buy these — which says the problem was never demand, it was that the men holding them waited.

Two owners went their own way. Brian Clemens kept Chase Brown at a 3rd over Tyler Warren at a 9th, and the chart sent the bill; the Guardians sold Travis Etienne, the bigger contract, to buy a live 6th and kept Egbuka instead. Both are defensible. Both will be quoted back at them in December.

The 2026 draft order

Set at the draft order reveal, and now fully settled. What follows is the board after the deadline — every pick trade applied and every keeper burn subtracted. Twenty–four of the 180 picks were consumed by Saturday’s declarations; the 156 below are the ones that were actually called on the day. If you are tracking who owns what from here, these are the assets that changed hands.

Kevin Flanagan now sits on the most capital in the league, 2,674, and it is a strange pile: three second–round picks — his own at 16, Patrick Hanna’s at 22 and Brian Clemens’ at 23 — survived the deadline untouched while both of his 3rds burned on keepers. Darryl Powell still holds the most picks, sixteen, even after burning two 6ths on Taylor and Lamb.

At the other end, the Judkins trade and two keeper burns left Patrick Hanna with the least capital on the board, 1,800 across twelve picks — the price of pairing the league’s best contract with a bought second keeper. James Lombardi holds the fewest picks, eleven, after spending two of them buying his keeper card outright.

Why rounds 3 to 9 are the ones that matter

Across 179 keeper selections since 2017, 68% of every keeper this league has ever declared cost a pick between the 3rd and the 9th round. Rounds 14 and 15 have produced four keepers in nine years combined. Two men have ever been kept at a 1st, both back when the two–round penalty could push a 3rd–round keeper up that far. Under today's rules it cannot happen.

That is why those middle rounds carry a premium in the chart above. A 5th–round pick is not just a player, it is a lottery ticket on a two–year contract, and this league has cashed that ticket about 30% of the time.

One thing that will cost someone a pick this year

Keepers come out of the pool before the draft does. With 24 players — many of them first and second–round talents — removed, everyone left slides. Expect real players to go one to two rounds earlier than raw ADP suggests. If you are drafting off a printed ESPN cheat sheet on draft night without adjusting, you will reach on everybody and not notice.

What the keepers do to all of this

The received wisdom in this league is that a pick here gets you the player who would have gone about two rounds later in a normal redraft. Twenty–four men come off the board before anybody picks, so everything slides. That is roughly right — and it is badly wrong exactly where the money is.

The reason is that the keepers are not spread evenly. Only seven of the twenty–four declared keepers are top–24 ADP players. Fourteen of them — more than half the board — sit in ADP rounds three and four.

Through the first twelve picks the drift is about four spots — a third of a round. The top three ADP players in the game are not kept by anybody, so pick 1.01 here is pick 1.01 anywhere. By pick 24 the drift is a full round. By pick 60 it is a round and a half, and from there it settles at exactly two rounds and stays there.

Which means the conventional wisdom has it backwards at the point it matters most. First–round picks in this league are worth nearly what they are worth anywhere. The keeper tax is real, but it is paid in rounds three through eight, where the player you get is a round and a half worse than the slot suggests, and it is paid hardest by whoever is still shopping in the middle.

The chart above already accounts for this

Every value in the pick chart is now the redraft worth of the player actually available at that pick, plus that round's keeper premium. It is not the worth of the man who goes at that ADP, because he is usually gone.

The practical effect: a first–round pick is worth more, relative to everything else, than the old numbers said. Pick 1.01 used to price at 3.9 times a 4.01. It now prices at 5.1 times. Middle–round picks lost about a fifth of their value, and because a keeper costs you a pick, every keeper on the board got more valuable at the same time.

Wheeling and dealingEvery 2026 trade, seven years of history, and the waiver wire record

Every trade on the books since 2019, and what the waiver wire actually cost. If you have ever wondered whether the guy on the other end of a text message makes trades or just talks about them, this settles it. How a man trades is half his fingerprint. How he drafts is the rest.

The offseason just finished was the busiest this league has ever had before a draft: the three May swaps that turned dead contracts into franchise keepers, the Bowers heist in mid–August, and then four sales in the final 72 hours — Smith, Judkins, Etienne and Flowers — with the last of them clearing at 9:41 pm inside an extended deadline. Every one of them is below, priced. The history underneath it is why the phone rings for some of you and not for others: Sean Quincey and Dannie Walker have combined for ninety–two trades since 2019, better than a third of the league’s total; Ken Tinkham had made six in seven years before Saturday’s Etienne deal made it seven.

Ken Tinkham has been party to six trades since 2019. The next quietest owner has thirteen. Sean Quincey and Dannie Walker have combined for ninety–two — better than a third of every trade this league has made since 2019, between the two of them.

Forty–eight trades and six

Sean Quincey has been involved in forty–eight of the 143 trades on this page and has moved 109 assets doing it — more than double the league median. He trades in the offseason, he trades at the deadline, he trades in weeks nobody else is paying attention. Whatever engine runs this league's trade market, it is mostly him.

Ken Tinkham has made six, moving sixteen assets across seven seasons. Nine seasons in this league, the best open–draft grade of anyone on the board, and a trade history that would not fill a page. He has decided the draft is the whole game and the rest of you are a distraction.

The 2025 deadline week

Nine days in November did more to reshape rosters than the entire draft that preceded it. On 15 November James Lombardi sent Christian McCaffrey, a 9th and a 12th to Dannie Walker for a 3rd, a 10th and Nick Chubb — six pieces, the biggest deal of the year by volume.

Four days later Flanagan and Patrick Hanna swapped Amon–Ra St. Brown and Harold Fannin for Brock Bowers and Jauan Jennings, and Flanagan turned an 11th–round pick into a 2nd on the same handshake. That 2nd is pick 22 in the draft you are about to sit down for. Bowers did not last as his keeper — Flanagan flipped him to Dannie Walker for Drake London the following August, which is a trade of its own worth reading below. That is one November trade doing three jobs at once, and it is worth studying even if the player did not stick around.

The next day Dannie Walker and Jon Nairn traded three starters each — Purdy, Swift and Pitts for Kittle, Hurts and Collins. A week after that, Hanna and Lombardi swapped DK Metcalf for Davante Adams straight up and the market closed.

The waiver wireWhat every owner actually paid for his claims, 2022–2025

A reminder before the numbers: this is ESPN's play money. Every owner gets a fictional $100 acquisition budget to bid with, and it has nothing to do with the real hundred you put in the pot. What follows is what each owner actually paid for the claims he won. Losing bids cost nothing, however brave they looked on the Wednesday.

FAAB arrived in 2022. Since then the pattern has not moved: this league spends its play money. $616 went out in 2022, $718 in 2023, $613 in 2024, $776 in 2025 — and in every single one of those years at least two owners emptied the account entirely. The ceiling on a winning bid has climbed from $30 in 2024 to $50 in 2025.

There is more than one way to spend a hundred dollars. In 2022 James Lombardi spent his entire budget on a single claim and never bid again all year. Three seasons later he won nine claims and paid nothing for any of them.

The one that got kept

We do not track how many points a waiver pickup scores afterward — only whether ESPN's own record eventually calls it a keeper, which is as close to "this pickup won" as the data gets. Across every FAAB season, exactly one waiver claim cleared that bar the clean way: same owner won the claim and kept the player himself the next year. Jon Nairn won Jayden Reed for $0 in December 2023. By 2024 that $0 bid was a locked keeper. That is the entire find–a–diamond story this league has to tell so far — which says as much about how rarely a free pickup turns into a real asset as it does about Jon Nairn's eye.

Two ways to run out of money

Brian Clemens spent his entire 2025 budget on four players — $45 on C.J. Stroud, $40 on Christian Watson, and $15 between two others. Jon Nairn spent exactly the same hundred dollars across twenty–three claims, never bidding more than $10 on anything. Same outcome, opposite religion.

And then there is James Lombardi, who won nine claims in 2025 and paid nothing for any of them. Ken Tinkham won one, for $10.

Sixteen years of draftingCareer draft grades, tendencies and the best and worst picks ever made here

Every pick from 2010–2025 scored on what the player really produced that season, under our scoring, against what a pick in that spot was worth. 2,566 picks graded so far. Draft day is one exam. The keeper call is the other.

This year’s exam

Ken Tinkham is the best drafter this league has ever had — +735 across nine seasons — and he picks tenth; Patrick Hanna is the worst on record at −2,170 and picks third. Running backs have cost every owner money, −27.9 a pick over 751 open selections, and sixteen of the twenty worst picks ever made here were quarterbacks taken too early. This year’s board was the seventeenth exam; the sixteen before it are below.

Sixteen years of grades, 2010–2025Every pick scored, the best and worst of all time, and where each owner wins and loses by round
16Drafts graded, 2010–2025
2,566Picks scored
80%Of the twenty worst picks were quarterbacks
0Sum of every owner's score in a draft — it is zero–sum

How a pick gets a grade

Take a player's actual fantasy points that season under our settings — six–point passing touchdowns, half a point per ten passing yards, half–PPR, the yardage bonuses, our kicker table. Convert that to value over a replacement–level player at his position. Then compare it to what a pick in that slot returned on average that year.

Beat that number and you are positive. Because the expectation curve is fitted to each draft's own results, the twelve owners in any season sum to zero: you can only gain here at the expense of the other eleven.

What it does not see

This is drafting alone. Waivers, trades and lineup calls — a large share of any season — are invisible to it. Team defences are ungraded because the source data cannot score our D/ST rules, and the forty–yard touchdown bonuses are missing for the same reason.

A player who never took a snap that year scores zero, which is exactly what the pick was worth.

The open draft — keeper declarations removed

Two names deserve a word before you read the table. Ken Tinkham comes out on top of sixteen years of drafting and has still never played in a final, which makes him the best August owner and the most forgettable December one in league history. Beans sits fourth from bottom on the strength of the last two years alone; before 2018 he was comfortably positive, and his 2015 draft is the fourth–best anyone has ever had.

Keepers are a separate skill, priced elsewhere in this guide. Strip them out and what is left is what each owner did with a live board.

Most of this table rests on fourteen to sixteen seasons of drafting, which is enough to trust the gap between the top and bottom with real confidence. Two owners have far less: James Lombardi has drafted six times, and Kevin Clemens seven — with a decade–long gap in the middle. Treat their spots on the board with more caution than everyone else's.

Keepers are held out of these grades — what follows is the picks you actually made. The keeper era in this league starts in 2017; every pick before that was an open pick, so seasons from 2010 to 2016 are graded whole.

Sixteen years of habitsShow sixteen years of drafting habits, by owner

Every open pick this league has made since 2010, sorted by who made it and what they did with it. Not who drafts well — that is the previous section — but who reaches for a quarterback, who refuses to take a tight end, and which positions this league has been quietly setting money on fire at for sixteen years. Habits leave receipts. The grades collect them.

The league has a running back problem

Measured against what a pick at that slot normally returns, running backs have cost this league 20,995 points across 747 open picks — an average of -28.1 every time somebody calls one. That is not one owner's bad luck. All twelve owners are negative on running backs. Every single one.

Wide receivers come in at +3.0 a pick and tight ends at +22.6. In the first three rounds the gap is starker still: receivers run +21.2 a pick, running backs -15.5.

Kickers lead the table at +37.9 for a boring reason: they go around pick 170, where nothing is expected of a pick, and this league's kicker table pays them like real players. Running backs have no such excuse. Those picks get spent early, where a miss is expensive.

The extremes are genuinely extreme. James Lombardi takes his first quarterback around round five; Brian Haas waits until round eleven and a half. Six rounds apart on the same position, in the same league, with the same information.

Kevin Flanagan does not draft tight ends. His first one comes at round 12.8 on average — four full rounds later than anyone else, deep enough to be a philosophy rather than an oversight. It is worth noting he solved the problem this year by trading for Brock Bowers instead. Three titles and he still will not spend a pick on the position.

Ken Tinkham has never done it differently. Since 2020 he has not used a single first–, second– or third–round pick on a quarterback or a tight end. Not once. Backs and receivers, in some order, every single year. He grades out as the best open–draft owner in the league doing it — and has still never reached a final in nine seasons, which is the most Ken Tinkham sentence available.

Brian Haas is the most running–back–heavy starter in the league at 62% of early picks, with Kevin Clemens just behind. Given the table above, that is a habit worth a second look.

The keeper recordEvery declaration since 2017, scored

Every keeper declared between 2017–2025, 178 of them, scored the same way as a draft pick: what the player actually produced that year, against what the round he cost was worth. Every number so far has been building toward one place: the record book.

Why the declarations mattered

An ordinary draft pick is a coin flip: about half beat the slot they were taken at. A keeper beats his round three times in four, by an average of 39 points of value — which is why Saturday night was most of the edge available to anyone before a ball is kicked. Darryl Powell leads the league in keeper grading, +1,080 since 2017, and he just locked the two most valuable contracts on the board.

This is the single clearest number in the guide. An ordinary draft pick is a coin flip — about half beat the slot they were taken at. A keeper beats his round more than three times in four, by an average of 39 points of value. Declaring well is not a tiebreaker in this league; it is most of the edge available to you before the season starts.

What the good ones have in common

Almost none of them were the best player on the roster when they were declared. They were the cheapest good player — a receiver at a 6th, a tight end at a 13th, a quarterback at a 7th. The rounds that have produced the most value per declaration are the 6th, the 13th and the 9th, none of which is where the stars live.

The stars are usually first and second–round picks, and those can never be kept at all. That is the rule the whole market runs on.

What the bad ones have in common

Injury and position. Four of the five worst declarations ever were quarterbacks or a back who missed most of the year, and under our scoring a quarterback who misses time is not a disappointment — the twelfth–best quarterback in a season scores around 350 points, so anything less than a full year at the position is a hole you cannot fill from waivers.

Before you declare an expensive man at a rich round, ask what he is worth if he plays twelve games instead of seventeen. The cheap keeper survives that question. The expensive one usually does not.

The wall has room for one more

Season twenty–three is under way. One name goes up.

Twelve names are on the wall at the top of this page. Six of them got there more than once; none of them ever got there twice in a row. Every line in this book — 1,260 games, 143 trades, 2,776 picks — was written by somebody at this table, and most of it was written at somebody else’s expense.

The twenty–third season is writing itself now. Somebody’s eleventh–round keeper will look like a heist by October. Somebody’s second–round tight end will get quoted back at him for a decade. Darryl Powell will walk up to the wall nobody has ever climbed twice in a row — and eleven of you are waiting there to stop him — Eric Counihan gets the next swing, in Week 5, with the only roster in the league inside four points a week of Powell’s.

Appendix / Method

How the numbers work

Where every number came from, and how much to trust it.

Some of this guide is a record of what happened. Some of it is an estimate. They are kept separate on purpose, so you know how hard to lean on any given figure. That is the whole machine. One page left.

Measured — taken directly from league records

  • The 16 ESPN–era seasons of standings, records and points (2010–2025), from the final–standings pages. Champions from 2004 forward, from the early league records.
  • All 16 playoff brackets, seeds and scores.
  • Every keeper declared since 2017, and every pick of all sixteen ESPN–era drafts.
  • Weekly player statistics for every season since 2010, scored under our settings.
  • Every 2026 transaction through the Week 4 waiver run.
  • Scoring settings and the rulebook text.

Modelled — estimates, carrying real error

  • Weekly projections. Each roster is dropped into the lineup this league actually starts — one quarterback, one back, two receivers, a tight end, a back–or–receiver flex, a kicker and a defense — and the points–per–week curve is scaled so that the twelve projections average what the twelve teams have actually averaged through six weeks, 106.2 a game. Week–to–week variation is set at 24.8 points, measured from this season's own scores rather than assumed. Trade values move with that same scale, so the gap between two sides of a deal — which is what the evaluator grades — is unaffected by it.
  • The base pick curve. Pick 1.01 anchored at 1,000, decaying to about 45 at pick 180, log–interpolated. There is no published fantasy equivalent of the Jimmy Johnson chart. Any single cell is good to roughly ±15%.
  • The keeper premium. The bump each round gets for being a round that actually produces keepers here. Calibrated on our own history: the chance a pick in that round becomes a keeper, times the gap between the average kept player's value and that round's mid–pick value. It runs from +4 to +29.
  • Projected finish. Each owner’s three inputs — three–year average regular–season finish, 2026 keeper haul, and career draft grade — are standardized against the other eleven and combined at 45% form, 35% haul, 20% draft grade; the twelve totals are then ranked. Rerun after the declarations, so every projection reflects the exact–pick haul.
  • Surplus. Worth at his 2026 ADP slot, minus the value of the pick burned. For the twenty–four declared keepers that is the exact overall pick consumed on 29 August, priced off the same chart as the capital column; for everyone else it is the round’s mid–pick value, since no specific pick was ever burned. Both inputs carry the errors above, so treat ±30 as noise.
  • Expected value by draft slot. Used for the draft and keeper grades. Each season's own results are fitted to a curve of value against pick number, so every draft is graded against the board that league actually produced. Value over replacement uses the twelfth quarterback, thirtieth back, thirty–sixth receiver, twelfth tight end and twelfth kicker in a twelve–team year, and scales with the field when the league was smaller.

Not known — treat these with caution

  • The 2004–2009 standings. We have champions but no win–loss records, so every rate statistic in the record book is an ESPN–era figure.
  • ADP accuracy. Treat any single average–pick figure as approximate. Check it yourself before you trade on it.
  • Who owns which pick. A dozen pick trades have gone through this offseason and the overall numbers logged before the 29 May order change are stale. Check the ESPN draft board. This ledger prices players, not pick inventory.
  • Whether the swap market is finished. Three teams still hold stuck assets — Aura Farmers, Respect My Conglomerate and Stu The Assassin — and the clock runs out on the 29th.
  • The 2019 playoff high points winner. Blank in the rulebook. If you remember, tell the commissioner and we will fill it in.

A note on precision

Do not read these numbers to the point. A surplus of +215 and a surplus of +190 are the same number for practical purposes. What the model is good at is telling you that +215 and +25 are not remotely the same thing, and which side of a trade is getting the better of it. Use it to frame the argument, not to end it.

One small thing

Every number in here is checked against the league's own record, but this is a big, hand–built spreadsheet run by one guy after work. If something looks off, tell the commissioner and it gets fixed.
